strengths: The paper addresses a practical NLP problem: forecasting pretraining loss to support hyperparameter selection directly on the target model. The token-position decomposition provides an interpretable empirical description of how loss changes with context and training progress.

The experiments derive functional forms using small models and evaluate future-loss prediction on 468M, 1.2B, and 6.7B models. Figures 3 and 5 report substantial improvements over the tested baselines on both Pile and C4 validation data, providing evidence beyond retrospective curve-fitting accuracy.

The data-mixture application connects predictions to completed training runs. The selected mixtures improve reported final perplexity in all four model/dataset settings and improve 12 of 14 downstream benchmark comparisons. The equations, architecture tables, and pseudocode also help communicate the approach.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not isolate the benefit of token-position decomposition. The proposed predictor incorporates a flexible piecewise temporal function and the known cosine schedule, whereas the aggregate-loss baselines use simpler functions without that schedule information. After a0 and a1 are frozen, Eq. (10) reduces to a constant plus a2(N). A direct aggregate-loss baseline using the same temporal form, together with relevant schedule-aware predictors such as the cited Luo et al. (2025), is needed to substantiate the claimed source of improvement.

The central prediction procedure remains insufficiently specified for reliable reproduction. Algorithm 1, lines 29–30, applies calibration when Npred is at or below Nsep, contradicting Section 2.4, which requires observations beyond Nsep. The outlier-removal threshold, fitting initialization and constraints, and evaluation interval are also unspecified. These details materially affect extrapolation and need clarification, ideally accompanied by fitting code and loss traces.

The evidence for the positional functional-form comparison is internally inconsistent. Section 2.3 reports power-law R² below 0.75 for over 95% of checkpoints, while Table 9 reports R² above 0.95 for 67% of checkpoints in the 58M setting. Different experimental conditions could explain this, but none are identified; the discrepancy must be resolved.

The hyperparameter-selection evidence is preliminary. Selection uses only 10B of 400B tokens, or 2.5%, whereas the main forecasting experiments evaluate prefixes of 10–40%. The paper omits the actual candidate mixture vectors and candidate-level predicted versus realized losses. The final perplexity improvements are approximately 0.7–1.3%, without uncertainty estimates; averaging five adjacent checkpoints does not establish robustness across training runs.

The theoretical interpretations overreach the evidence. Appendix C excludes exponential decay by setting its additive offset to zero, although a shifted exponential can approach a positive loss floor. Equation (17) follows from manually freezing a0 and a1; it is a conditional property of the fitted model. Neither that identity nor three suppression strategies establishes that position-based reweighting is generally unnecessary.

The novelty and generality claims need narrowing. Kaplan et al. already examine training-step-dependent learning curves, so temporal evolution itself is not unexplored. Moreover, the GPT-NeoX, MoE, and linear-schedule extensions demonstrate retrospective fits rather than future-loss prediction. The strongest forecasting evidence concerns the tested Pile/cosine settings. The missing controls, conflicting results, and implementation ambiguities warrant revision before a sound and reproducible Findings recommendation.
